extracted.intended_audience: general readers, researchers, policymakers and media seeking information about the Christchurch mosque shootings
extracted.subtask_description: A comprehensive encyclopedia-style article summarising the 2019 Christchurch mosque shootings: events, livestream/video distribution, legal responses, copycat incidents, media and social-media reactions, inquiries, and subsequent policy changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of the livestream/video as 'objectionable' under New Zealand law
rubrics_metrics.description: The New Zealand Office of Film and Literature Classification quickly classified the livestreamed video as 'objectionable', making it a criminal offence in New Zealand to distribute, copy, or exhibit the video.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criminal penalties cited include up to 14 years' imprisonment for an individual, or up to $100,000 in fines for a corporation. Police, Muslim advocacy groups, and government agencies urged anyone who found the footage to take it down or report it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform content moderation and removal of extremist/violent content
rubrics_metrics.description: Various social media sites—including Facebook, YouTube, Reddit, and Twitter—said they were working to remove the video from their platforms and to remove content posted in support of the attacks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Facebook reported removal within minutes after notification, created a digital hash fingerprint to detect further uploads, and said it had blocked 1.5 million uploads of the video. Reddit banned subreddits (e.g., 'WatchPeopleDie', 'Gore') for glorifying violence. Examples illustrate platform takedown practices and automated/detection tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media restraint guidance regarding broadcasting violent footage
rubrics_metrics.description: Police urged media organisations not to show the footage; despite this, several media organisations broadcast parts of the video up to the point the attacker entered the building.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some broadcasters were criticised and took actions (e.g., Sky Television New Zealand temporarily stopped syndication of a network after it showed footage). The item functions as an editorial standard: avoid showing violent footage and comply with police/community requests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of technical/detection standards (digital fingerprinting) to prevent reuploading
rubrics_metrics.description: Facebook created a digital hash fingerprint to detect further uploads after the video had been propagated on other sites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as a practical mitigation practice for platforms to prevent re-distribution of extremist violent video; Microsoft also proposed industry-wide standards to flag such content quickly and a joint project to manage spread across platforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposed and enacted legal obligations on content providers to remove violent imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Australia introduced legislation that would fine content providers and potentially imprison their executives if they do not remove violent imagery of these types of attacks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Governments and world leaders called on tech companies to take responsibility for extremist content. The Christchurch Call summit urged major technology companies to step up efforts to combat violent extremism; the initiative had state and company signatories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminal prosecution standards for sharing or possessing the video/manifesto
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals have been arrested and prosecuted for possessing, sharing, or doctoring copies of the video or manifesto under domestic law (e.g., Films, Videos, and Publications Classification Act 1993 in New Zealand).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Philip Arps was indicted and pleaded guilty to sharing the video under the Films, Videos, and Publications Classification Act 1993 and was sentenced to 21 months' imprisonment (released under monitoring conditions). Other people were arrested, tried, or convicted for possession, sharing, doctoring footage, or related threats.

rubrics_metrics.name: ISP/site-blocking measures to restrict access to sites hosting the footage
rubrics_metrics.description: At least three Internet service providers in New Zealand blocked access to 8chan and other sites related to the attacks, and temporarily blocked other sites hosting the video until they complied with takedown requests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This represents an operational policy lever used by states/ISPs to limit online distribution pending compliance with requests to remove extremist material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gun-law and firearm-policy reforms following the attack
rubrics_metrics.description: In response to the attack, New Zealand reclassified and then banned some semi-automatic weapons, introduced the Arms (Prohibited Firearms, Magazines, and Parts) Amendment Act 2019, and ran a buy-back scheme for affected firearms and parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cites the timeline (announcement of changes on the day of the attack; legislation introduced 1 April 2019 and passed on 10 April 2019), buy-back scheme metrics (e.g., numbers of hand-ins and parts collected), and political debate about the scheme's effectiveness. This is a substantive regulatory outcome described as part of the official response.
